source.title: Steering Vectors are an Adversarial Attack Surface
source.authors: Abzal Aidakhmetov; Donato Crisostomi; Tommaso Mencattini; Adrian Robert Minut; Iacopo Masi; Emanuele Rodolà

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present, including appendices.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses a different intervention from the original: it poisons contrastive steering vectors to align them with a mean-difference anti-refusal direction, then tests harmful-prompt refusal and the effect of projecting that component out.
record.gate_note: The study reports attack success, benign attribute compliance, defense results, and an all-step protocol check. It also reports direction-cosine results, but those measure alignment rather than refusal behavior; they are not included as rows. Values used to select layers and steering weights are not results.
record.test_reason: The study works in a new setting: poisoned contrastive steering vectors applied at one layer during prefill. It uses the Arditi-style mean-difference direction r as its attack target, so the raw ASR results largely measure its own method. Three results do bear on whether that direction carries the jailbreak. Adding vectors partly aligned with r raises harmful-prompt ASR. Projecting r out of the poisoned vectors removes most of that lift. Capping alignment with r during optimisation keeps ASR near the clean level. Together these test V1's causal claim and V3's mechanism claim for this one attack type.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that contrastive steering datasets can be stealthily poisoned, by about 4–6% token swaps, to align vectors with the anti-refusal direction. The poisoned vectors reach 0.20–0.55 ASR (+19 to +51 pp) while keeping the benign attribute. Projecting out the refusal direction recovers about 82% of the ASR gap, and a cosine-threshold screen resists adaptive attackers in the cell tested.
record.recipe_differences: The study estimates an anti-refusal direction using a harmful-versus-harmless mean difference, but attacks by poisoning attribute steering datasets and applies the resulting vector at one selected layer during prefill. It does not perform the original all-layer, all-position ablation or isolated direction addition.
record.method_sensitivity: Results depend on model family, target attribute, selected layer and bundled steering weight. The paper also reports a different outcome under prefill versus all-step steering and a strong reduction in attack success when cosine alignment is capped.

fits_no_version.finding: Poisoned vectors keep their declared benign attribute behaviour, both under the poisoning itself and under the defense.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Poisoned steering vectors can preserve their declared benign attribute while raising harmful-prompt ASR.

record.code_released: The paper states that attack, defense, and evaluation code is released under the MIT license; URL not stated.
record.problems: Only two model families, up to 8B parameters, and English harmful/harmless prompts are tested. One combination (Gemma-2-2B-IT lowercase) has weak clean attribute compliance (AC = 0.14). The main per-combination plots do not state all exact values in the text. The benign check measures the target attribute, not broad capability.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row cap. Per-combination vector-cosine and norm-ratio plots were not entered because they measure geometry or norm rather than refusal behavior; the paper reports their aggregate ranges in Sections 4.3–4.4 and Figure 3/Figure 5.

untested.parts: No ablation of the direction at all layers and positions on the model itself. No addition of the isolated refusal direction to induce refusal. No broad capability check.
Only an attack constructed to align with r was tested; prompt-level jailbreaks were not. No training against ablation.
No multi-direction comparison, though about 18% of the lift survives orthogonalisation on average.

missing.what: Per-combo defended ASR and gap recovered: about 38% and 36% for Gemma spanish and french, versus 82–114% for the other combos.
Clean-vector control under the defense: |ΔASR| ≤ 0.05 on the seven well-behaved combos.
Clean ASR baselines for r7 (0.04) and r8 (about 0.05), derivable from the text.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source. The attack is built on r, so the raw ASR rows are partly the method's own performance. The causal evidence comes from the defense and the cosine-cap ablation. The cap sweep was run only on Llama lowercase.

versions.untested_parts: Does not ablate the direction from every layer and position or add the isolated refusal direction; does not test broad general capability. Its projection defense removes a component from a poisoned steering vector.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration is evaluated.
Tests poisoned steering vectors that add an anti-refusal component, not other jailbreak mechanisms; does not train models against the ablation.
Does not compare single-direction explanations with affine, cone, or multiple-direction accounts.
Does not separately measure harmfulness judgment and refusal decision.
Spanish and French are steering attributes, not tests of direction transfer across languages or model stages.
Does not vary refusal-training method or timing.

relation.reason: The projection and cosine-cap results test whether the refusal-direction component drives the refusal suppression.

tranche.reason: The setting is new (poisoned contrastive steering vectors, prefill, one layer). Beyond the attack ASR, the study reports results on whether r carries the effect: projecting r out (Section 4.7) and a cosine-cap sweep (Appendix E). That rules out T4. The question is security, not refusal mechanism, so T3 fits better than T2.

source_check.notes: In this paper r is the anti-refusal direction (harmless − harmful, = −r_ref), and Appendix E switches to cos(v, −r) notation. The per-combo gap-recovered values (38, 36, 82, 114, 108, 101, 92, 84%) are Figure 4a annotations with an inferred combo mapping. The body text gives only the 82% mean, 0.09–0.51 reduction and 'at or below baseline on three combos'. No capability benchmarks (only attribute compliance and GPT-2 perplexity); models are 8B or smaller.

statements.correction: r = mean h(harmless) − mean h(harmful), M = 128 per side, oriented so adding it suppresses refusal (r = −r_ref); poisoned cos(v, r) 0.22–0.59. Llama has_bold_only: 0.49 ± 0.04, ΔASR +0.44 (clean ASR not stated). Other numbers match the text: 0.25→0.49 ± 0.07; 0.55 ± 0.13 vs 0.04; 0.02→0.43; 0.06→0.40; 0.09–0.51; 0.057 ± 0.006 vs 0.043.
statements.problem: The conditions say r is a harmful-minus-harmless mean difference. The study's r is harmless minus harmful (anti-refusal, r = −r_ref, Eq. 2), which is why the cosines are positive. 'About 0.05' for Llama has_bold_only is derived from ΔASR +0.44, not stated. The per-combo 82–114% comes from Figure 4a annotations; the body text gives only the 82% mean.

statements.correction: Figure 4a gap-recovered annotations: 38%, 36% (Gemma spanish, french by position); the other six are 82–114%. Section 4.7 gives a mean of 82% and ASR reductions of 0.09–0.51.
statements.problem: 36% and 38% are Figure 4a annotations, not body text. Their assignment to Gemma spanish/french comes from annotation order in the extracted text, so it is likely but not certain.

statements.correction: Gemma spanish/french: about 62–64% of the lift survives projection (Figure 4a). Other six combos: 82–114% recovered; three end at or below clean.
statements.problem: Right for Gemma spanish/french. On the other six combos, projecting r out recovers 82–114% of the gap, so for this study the direction accounts for most of the effect elsewhere.

statements.correction: Projecting r out removes on average 82% of the poisoned-vs-clean ASR gap (Section 4.7).
